notes.text: White's queen eyes f5, so skip Bf5 and Bg4; play g6, dxc4 or e6 instead.
This is the Exchange Variation: White is slightly better because your light bishop has trouble developing.
This is the position you want: meet every Qb3 with Qb6 and learn to play queenless middlegames.
Your knight hits the c3 knight, forcing White to trade or push it away with e4.
These two moves define the Slav: solid, but developing your light bishop is hard and White can target your queenside pawns.
This move defines the Semi-Slav: you threaten to take on c4 and defend it with b5.
Semi-Slav with Bg5: you choose between taking on c4 or chasing the bishop with h6. Both are sharp.
The game is very sharp and complicated and needs more analysis to play properly.
White avoids the sharp Slav and wants Bf4 then e3; you can seek tactics with an early Qb6.
This is the usual Pure Slav position: you counter the center and press on the b6-f2 diagonal.
This line is tricky: played carelessly, you can lose quickly, so know the theory well.
White will win the c4 pawn back eventually, but you gain time to develop your pieces.
The e3 pawn boxes in White's dark bishop, and opening the center early can turn this calm line sharp.
White is following his plan of retaking the center with e4.
You will answer with ...c5 to keep the balance in the center.
Nc3 stops Bf5, so your best reply is e6, transposing into the Semi-Slav.
The knight looks odd on c1, but it is heading for the fine b3 square.
White has a good grip on the center; a good plan is Bh5, pinning the knight.
The first Slav problem is solved: your light bishop is out on its most active diagonal.
White chooses now: e5 is the sharpest and most played, d5 is calmer, while castling or Bg5 are worse.
Always take on c4 when you can: the queen was guarding that pawn, so you lose no time.
Bb7 is more precise than Be7: it prepares against a painful Ne5 from White.
Your b5 pawn guards the c4 pawn, so White must fight to win it back.
A rich middlegame: what matters is understanding the Slav ideas so you reach positions you know.
Your far-advanced queenside pawns are like mini queens; White will try to go around them and attack your king.
Bb4 is more sound than Be7: it is active, and White's a-pawn cannot kick it away.
With a4, White gave up the e4 square for a while; your bishop develops naturally and you stand well.
You fianchetto the dark bishop and back up f5 so your light bishop can develop.
This typical Exchange Slav position is calmer and less rich than the main lines, but still gives you good ideas.
You are a pawn up but cramped, while White has kingside attacking chances; you play on the queenside.
This keeps your bishop pair and your grip on e4, so White can't build a full center.
This is the Pure Slav: you plan ...b5 to keep the extra pawn and give your light bishop room.
Very sharp: your king is still in the center, but your bishops and the g-file give real kingside chances.
The knight move looks silly but isn't: White is a pawn down and must attack, so careful with h6.
This is White's strongest move here; other moves give White little counterplay.
Recommended: take on c4 when a queen or bishop can guard it, or play e6 for Semi-Slav positions.
